title: The phase plane
objectives: Sketch trajectories in the phase plane for nodes, saddles, spirals and centres.

screens.title: Plot $y$ against $x$
screens.prose: Take $x' = x + 2y$, $y' = 2x + y$. Instead of plotting each against time, plot the point $(x(t), y(t))$: the **phase plane**. Arrows show the velocity; the curve from your start runs forwards and backwards. Drag the start.
screens.question: Along which line do the paths leave the origin?

options.why: Paths come **in** along $(1, -1)$; run forwards and they turn away along $(1, 1)$.
Start on the axis at $(1, 0)$ and watch it bend away.
Only one direction is a straight escape; the others curve towards it.

feedback.correct: They come in along $(1, -1)$ and leave along $(1, 1)$: a **saddle**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start near the origin and follow the forward end.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue 3 on $(1, 1)$ and $-1$ on $(1, -1)$. Growth wins along $(1, 1)$, decay along $(1, -1)$.

screens.title: Where is it at $t = 0.5$?
screens.prose: From $(1, 0) = \tfrac12(1, 1) + \tfrac12(1, -1)$ the solution is $\mathbf{x}(t) = \tfrac12e^{3t}(1, 1) + \tfrac12e^{-t}(1, -1)$, as in lesson 10.
screens.question: What is $x(0.5)$, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the first components of both terms.

byKey.y: That is $y(0.5)$: the decaying part enters with a minus sign there.
byKey.grow: You kept only the growing part; add $\tfrac12e^{-0.5}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{x}(0.5) = (2.5441, 1.9376)$. The $e^{-t}$ part is already small, so the point hugs the $(1, 1)$ line.

screens.title: A stable node
screens.prose: Lesson 10's two-factor model, $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}-2&2\\0&-0.5\end{pmatrix}$: both eigenvalues negative. Every path heads into the origin. Drag the start and watch the last stretch of each path.
screens.question: Along which direction do paths arrive at the origin?

options.why: The $e^{-2t}$ part dies first, so what is left points along $(4, 3)$.

options.text: Straight in, from wherever they start
options.why: Only starts on an eigenvector come in straight.
Real eigenvalues give no turning.

hints.text: The two parts decay at rates 2 and 0.5.
What remains is a multiple of $(4, 3)$.

feedback.correct: The fast part vanishes first, so paths arrive tangent to $(4, 3)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which part of $c_1e^{-2t}\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2e^{-0.5t}\mathbf{v}_2$ survives longest?

explain.text: All paths enter tangent to the slow eigenvector: a **stable node**. With both eigenvalues positive the arrows reverse: an unstable node.

screens.title: A spiral
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\-2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $-1 \pm 2i$. The imaginary part turns the point once every $2\pi/2 = \pi$; the real part shrinks it by $e^{-t}$.
screens.question: By what factor does the distance from the origin shrink in one full turn, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.correct: One turn takes $\pi$, so the factor is $e^{-\pi} = 0.0432$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A turn takes $2\pi/2 = \pi$; shrink by $e^{-1}$ per unit time.

byKey.e1: That is one unit of time, not one turn.

explain.text: Each turn takes $\pi$ and shrinks by $e^{-\pi} = 0.0432$: a **stable spiral**. A positive real part would grow it instead.

screens.title: Which way round?
screens.prose: Eigenvalues say how fast a spiral turns, not which way. One velocity does: at $(1, 0)$ the velocity is $\mathbf{A}(1, 0)$, the first column of $\mathbf{A}$.
screens.question: For $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\-2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, which way does the spiral turn?

options.why: At $(1, 0)$ the velocity $(-1, -2)$ points down. Down from the positive $x$ axis is clockwise.
Complex eigenvalues always turn.
Every path of a linear spiral turns the same way.

hints.text: The velocity at $(1, 0)$ is the first column.
Moving down from the positive $x$ axis is clockwise.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\mathbf{A}(1, 0)$ and see which way it points.

explain.text: At $(1, 0)$ the point moves down: clockwise. The sign of the bottom-left entry, here $-2$, decides it for any spiral.

screens.title: Closed orbits of a centre
screens.prose: l9's undamped oscillator, $x' = y$, $y' = -4x$, has eigenvalues $\pm 2i$: a **centre**. Show its orbits are the ellipses $4x^2 + y^2 = \text{const}$. One line is wrong; leave it out.
screens.question: Put the argument in order.

lines.text: $= 0$, so $H$ is constant and each orbit is an ellipse

lines.why: $x$ and $y$ depend on $t$: the chain rule brings in $x'$ and $y'$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $H$ along the solution with the chain rule.

byKey.x: You differentiated as if $x$ and $y$ were the variables. Along a path they depend on $t$.

explain.text: A conserved $H$ means every path stays on one level curve, an ellipse here. Nothing spirals in or out.

screens.title: Same eigenvalues, other way round
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix}-1&-2\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are also $-1 \pm 2i$. A colleague says it must turn the same way as the last spiral.
screens.question: Which way does $\mathbf{B}$'s spiral turn?

options.why: You read the turning from the eigenvalues. $\mathbf{B}(1, 0) = (-1, 2)$ points up: anticlockwise.
The order of a conjugate pair carries no direction.
Complex eigenvalues always turn.

hints.text: Ignore the eigenvalues; compute one velocity.
Up from the positive $x$ axis is anticlockwise.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the velocity at $(1, 0)$.

byKey.cw: You read the turning from the eigenvalues, which are the same for both. Check $\mathbf{B}(1, 0) = (-1, 2)$: it points up.

explain.text: $\mathbf{B}$ is the transpose of the last matrix: same eigenvalues, opposite turning. The eigenvalues give speed and decay; one velocity gives the direction.

screens.title: A zero eigenvalue
screens.prose: Take $x' = 0$, $y' = -y$: eigenvalues 0 and $-1$. Drag the start anywhere.
screens.question: Where are the equilibria?

options.why: At $(2, 0)$ both $x'$ and $y'$ are 0 too.
Every point with $y = 0$ is still.
On the $y$ axis, $y' = -y \ne 0$ except at the origin.

feedback.correct: $y = 0$ makes both derivatives 0: a line of equilibria.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find every point where $x' = 0$ and $y' = 0$.

explain.text: With eigenvalue 0 the eigenvector $(1, 0)$ is a whole line of equilibria. Each path drops straight onto it, so the picture is none of the four types.

screens.title: Four pictures
screens.prose:
For $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ the eigenvalues name the picture:

| eigenvalues | picture |
|---|---|
| real, same sign | node (stable if negative) |
| real, opposite signs | saddle |
| $\alpha \pm i\beta$, $\alpha \ne 0$ | spiral (stable if $\alpha < 0$) |
| $\pm i\beta$ | centre |
screens.question: Eigenvalues $-3$ and $2$: which picture?

options.why: Opposite signs: one direction grows.
Real eigenvalues do not turn.
A centre needs purely imaginary eigenvalues.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the signs of the two eigenvalues.

explain.text: One eigenvalue pulls in and the other pushes out. Paths come in along one eigenvector and leave along the other.

screens.question: Complete `trajectory` and `turning`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def trajectory(A, x0, ts):
    """Array of shape (len(ts), 2): x(t) for x' = A x, x(0) = x0."""
    vals, V = np.linalg.eig(np.asarray(A, dtype=float))
    c = np.linalg.solve(V, np.asarray(x0, dtype=float))
    ts = np.asarray(ts, dtype=float)
    return np.real((V @ (c[:, None] * np.exp(np.outer(vals, ts)))).T)

def turning(A):
    """'clockwise' or 'anticlockwise'; ValueError if the eigenvalues are real."""
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    tau, det = np.trace(A), np.linalg.det(A)
    if tau * tau - 4 * det >= 0:
        raise ValueError("real eigenvalues: no turning")
    return "anticlockwise" if A[1, 0] > 0 else "clockwise"
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They check positions, the conserved $4x^2 + y^2$, three directions as text and one ValueError. The first run loads NumPy.

hints.text: `np.exp(np.outer(vals, ts))` has one column per time.
At $(1, 0)$ the velocity's $y$ part is $\mathbf{A}_{21}$: positive means anticlockwise.

feedback.correct: A vectorised solution, checked against the centre's conserved quantity, and the direction from one entry.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Use `np.outer(vals, ts)` for every $\lambda t$ at once, and raise when $\tau^2 - 4\Delta \ge 0$.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with code that returns.

explain.text:
`np.outer(vals, ts)` is a 2 by n array of $\lambda_kt$. Scaling each row by $c_k$ and multiplying by $\mathbf{V}$ gives every $\mathbf{x}(t)$.

screens.title: Hold the difference
screens.prose: Two spreads move as $x' = x + 2y$, $y' = 2x + y$. Their sum $s = x + y$ obeys $s' = 3s$ and runs away. Their difference $d = x - y$ obeys $d' = -d$ and reverts. A trader holds the difference.
screens.question: What is the half-life of the difference, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the two equations: $d' = (x + 2y) - (2x + y)$.

byKey.sum: That is $\ln 2/3$, the doubling time of the sum.
byKey.one: $1/|\lambda|$ is not a half-life; multiply by $\ln 2$.

explain.text: $d' = -x + y = -d$: half-life $\ln 2 = 0.6931$. The difference is the saddle's stable eigenvector $(1, -1)$. In `coint` (Stage 2) this becomes cointegration.

ideas: The phase plane plots $(x(t), y(t))$; arrows give the velocity $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ and paths never cross.
Real eigenvalues of one sign give a node, of opposite signs a saddle; $\alpha \pm i\beta$ gives a spiral, $\pm i\beta$ a centre.
The direction of turning comes from one velocity, such as $\mathbf{A}(1, 0)$, never from the eigenvalues.

options.text: Through one point there is one velocity, so only one path

options.why: At the crossing the two paths would need two velocities, but $\mathbf{A}(1, 1)$ is one vector.

options.text: They may cross only at a centre
options.why: Centre orbits are nested ellipses; they never cross.

options.text: They may cross only at a saddle
options.why: Saddle paths approach the equilibrium but never cross elsewhere.

feedback.correct: Uniqueness: each point has one velocity, so one path.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many velocities does a point have?

explain.text: Two paths crossing would leave the crossing point in two directions. Paths may meet only at an equilibrium, and only as $t \to \pm\infty$.

A saddle needs opposite signs.
Real eigenvalues do not turn.
